questions.stem: A 26-year-old male presented with diarrhea. He also had some blood in his stool, tenesmus, and a mucoid discharge from his anus. He had had unprotected receptive anal intercourse 1 week earlier. Investigations: 4th generation HIV Ag/Ab negative Syphilis EIA negative Urine NAAT for gonorrhea and chlamydia negative Rectal NAAT testing positive for C. trachomatis, negative for N. gonorrhoeae
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Benzathine penicillin G for one dose
Cefixime orally in a single dose
Doxycycline for 7 days plus one dose of azithromycin

questions.explanation: Doxycycline for 21 days LGV can result in proctitis and proctocolitis. This may manifest as tenesmus, rectal bleeding, and mucoid discharge from the rectum. Laboratory diagnostics to distinguish LGV serovars of C. trachomatis are not widely available. The patient should be treated for LGV based upon the clinical presentation and positive C. trachomatis by NAAT . Treatment course for LGV proctitis is doxycycline 100 mg BD for 21 days.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q11

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman presented for antenatal care at 6/40 weeks pregnant. She was sexually active, with 5 casual male partners in the last year. Investigations: 4th generation HIV Ag/Ab negative Syphilis EIA negative Vaginal swab NAAT negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, positive for Chlamydia trachomatis One gram of azithromycin was administered orally for one dose.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Give a stat dose of ceftriaxone IM
Give an additional 1 gram of azithromycin in 4 weeks
Give weekly suppressive azithromycin 1 gram until delivery
Repeat Chlamydia NAAT at 36/40 or before delivery
Repeat Chlamydia NAAT in 4 weeks for test of cure

questions.explanation: Repeat Chlamydia NAAT in 4 weeks for test of cure Test of cure for Chlamydia is recommended during pregnancy. This recommendation was put in place to prevent the severe sequelae that can occur in mothers and neonates if infection persists. Repeat screening in the 3rd trimester may be warranted based upon patient risk. However, it is not the best of the options.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q10

a) Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, and L3.
b) (1) Inguinal/femoral lymphadenopathy forming a bubo (with the characteristic "groove sign"). (2) Proctitis/proctocolitis (severe rectal infection, mainly in MSM). [Secondary systemic illness with fever, headache and myalgias is an acceptable alternative.]

parts.text: How would you manage mom and baby?
What is the rationale for treating the baby?

questions.model_answer:
a) Mom: azithromycin and erythromycin are excluded (macrolide anaphylaxis), and doxycycline/ofloxacin/levofloxacin are contraindicated in pregnancy, so treat with amoxicillin 500 mg PO tid x7 days; obtain a test of cure by NAAT 3-4 weeks after therapy (recommended for all treated pregnant women). Evaluate/treat sexual partners. Baby: prophylaxis (topical erythromycin ointment) does NOT prevent chlamydial transmission, so provide close monitoring for neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis (onset 5-12 days) and pneumonia (before 8 weeks); if signs develop, confirm with conjunctival/nasopharyngeal DFA or NAAT and treat with oral erythromycin base 50 mg/kg/day divided qid x14 days.
b) To prevent/limit the complications of perinatally acquired C. trachomatis, namely neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis (a cause of ophthalmia neonatorum, 30-50% of exposed infants) and chlamydial infant pneumonia (11-20% of exposed infants).

cohort_answer.text: A) Mom: allergic to azithro, no doxy or FQ in pregnancy/lactation; Amoxicillin 500mg PO TID x7 days (similar efficacy to azithro); test of cure 3-4 weeks after tx complete in all pregnant women when using penicillin; also test for gonorrhea, syphilis, HIV at delivery, notify public health. Baby: close follow up monitoring for neonatal chlamydia (conjunctivitis, pneumonia); if develop sx, swab conjunctiva or NP and tx if positive. B) Minimize complications of neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis (cause of ophthalmia neonatorum) or neonatal pneumonia.

questions.model_answer:
a) Perinatally acquired Chlamydia trachomatis infection: neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum) with chlamydial pneumonia (staccato cough, afebrile). Gonococcal ophthalmia is the main differential.
b) (1) Conjunctival swab for Chlamydia DFA or NAAT plus Gram stain/culture to exclude N. gonorrhoeae; (2) Nasopharyngeal NAAT or culture for C. trachomatis (pneumonia); (3) NAAT/culture for N. gonorrhoeae given the shared risk and purulent discharge (chest radiograph typically shows interstitial infiltrates with hyperinflation and peripheral eosinophilia is characteristic).
c) Oral erythromycin base 50 mg/kg/day divided into four doses for 14 days (topical therapy alone is inadequate as it fails to clear nasopharyngeal carriage; efficacy ~80% and a second course may be needed).
d) Evaluate and treat the mother (and her partners): azithromycin 1 g PO single dose for C. trachomatis; because of no prenatal care and high concomitant gonorrhea risk, add empiric ceftriaxone for N. gonorrhoeae pending results.

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Ophthalmia neonatorum, Gonococcal vs Chlamydia conjunctivitis (chlamydia more common). Tests: Conjunctival swab for culture/gram stain (gonococcal, chlamydia); throat swab for culture/gram stain; throat swab for NAAT (chlamydia and gonorrhea). Baby treatment: CRO/CTX IM x1 (ceftriaxone preferred unless significant hyperbilirubinemia) for gonococcal disease; erythromycin x14 days for chlamydia pneumonia (given cough). Mother treatment: CRO 250mg IM x1 + azithromycin x1 (treats gonorrhea given high concomitant chlamydia rates); in high risk cases (no prenatal care, substance use, hx STIs) can treat pre-emptively while awaiting micro results.

questions.model_answer:
(1) Neisseria gonorrhoeae - ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose plus azithromycin 1 g PO single dose; do not use fluoroquinolones unless susceptibility proven; test of cure in MSM/pharyngeal disease.
(2) Chlamydia trachomatis - doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily for 7 days, or azithromycin 1 g PO single dose.
(3) Mycoplasma genitalium - azithromycin 500 mg PO day 1 then 250 mg PO daily days 2-5; moxifloxacin 400 mg PO daily for 7 days if previously azithromycin-treated or macrolide resistance (14 days if M. genitalium-associated PID).
(4) Trichomonas vaginalis - metronidazole 2 g PO single dose, or 500 mg PO twice daily for 7 days; treat current partners.
(Ureaplasma urealyticum - doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily for 7 days; Mycoplasma hominis is not an established cause of urethritis.)

cohort_answer.text: N. gonorrhoeae - ceftriaxone 250mg IM + 1g Azithromycin. C. trachomatis - azithromycin 1g PO or doxy 100mg PO BID x7d. Trichomonas vaginalis - metronidazole 2g x1 or 500mg PO BID x7d. Mycoplasma genitalium - Azithromycin 500mg x1 then 250mg PO x2-5d (if previously treated with azithro, Moxi 400mg daily x7d; if PID, Moxi 400 x14d); NAAT is diagnostic test of choice, routine screening not recommended. Ureaplasma urealyticum - doxycycline 100mg PO BID x7 days (no PHAC guideline; Sanford: doxy or azithro 1g x1).

questions.model_answer:
a) Neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis (Neisseria gonorrhoeae) - hyperacute bilateral purulent discharge within 24-48 h of delivery, exudate so profuse it reappears immediately after the eye is cleaned, often with conjunctival membranes; may rapidly invade intact cornea causing ulceration/perforation.
b) Neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis (Chlamydia trachomatis) - unilateral or bilateral discharge beginning 5-14 days after delivery, watery then mucopurulent/bloody, no follicular response in the neonate; the most frequent cause of neonatal conjunctivitis in the United States.
c) Conjunctival scraping/swab (must include conjunctival epithelial cells) for Gram stain and bacterial culture to identify N. gonorrhoeae, plus nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT) for C. trachomatis, which is more sensitive than conventional methods; PCR/Giemsa if HSV is suspected.

cohort_answer.text: Rapid bilateral purulent conjunctivitis (pus recurs immediately after wiping) = gonococcal conjunctivitis. Onset 5-14 days after delivery = C. trachomatis inclusion conjunctivitis. Diagnosis is clinical, confirmed by lab testing: Gram stain and culture (chocolate agar and Thayer-Martin media for gonorrhea, blood agar for other organisms); Giemsa stain for chlamydial suspicion, though NAAT now more commonly used (less expensive, less labor than viral culture). Newborns with suspected C. trachomatis infection should have samples drawn from both conjunctivae and oropharynx; swabs should include conjunctival epithelial cells since C. trachomatis is an obligate intracellular organism.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Conjunctival scraping/swab for Gram stain and culture for N. gonorrhoeae (and other bacteria). (2) Conjunctival specimen containing epithelial cells for C. trachomatis NAAT (more sensitive than conventional methods); consider HSV PCR on the same site. (3) Blood culture (plus CSF if disseminated disease is suspected) to detect the rare but severe disseminated gonococcal infection.
b) (1) Rhinitis. (2) Proctitis. (3) Disseminated gonococcal infection - arthritis, meningitis, pneumonia/septicemia, which can be fatal; chlamydial pneumonitis and otitis media are also complications not covered by topical therapy.
c) Ceftriaxone, single dose 25-50 mg/kg IV or IM, not exceeding 125 mg, with hospitalization and hourly saline irrigation of the conjunctival fornices; topical antibiotics if corneal involvement cannot be excluded.
d) (1) Treat for gonorrhoea with ceftriaxone. (2) Treat for concurrent chlamydia with oral erythromycin or tetracycline for 1 week (tetracycline avoided in breastfeeding/pregnant women); sexual partners must be treated as well.

questions.model_answer:

b) (1) Conjunctival scraping for Gram stain showing gram-negative intracellular diplococci. (2) Conjunctival culture on chocolate/selective (Thayer-Martin) medium, with blood agar for other bacteria. questions.question_raw: 27-year old man with chlamydia, gonorrhea and treponemal test positive. His RPR is 1:256, w (NOTE: did not specify location of Chlamydia/gonorrhea infection, or whether patient is MSM etc) per PHAC

parts.text: What three drugs would you treat with? Include dose, route, duration.
What are two reasons for the RPR not decreasing four-fold at 12 months, other than incorrect clinical staging at diagnosis?

parts_raw.text: What 3 drugs would you treat with? Include dose, route, duration
What are 2 reasons for RPR not decreasing 4 fold at 12 months, other than incorrect clinical staging at diagnosis

questions.model_answer: a) Three drugs: (1) Syphilis — benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose (high titre >1:32 is managed as early syphilis). (2) Chlamydia — doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily for 7 days. (3) Gonorrhea — ceftriaxone (per PHAC) 250 mg IM single dose. b) Two reasons: (1) Reinfection. (2) Unrecognized neurosyphilis (CNS involvement) — also consider treatment failure or a serofast/slow serologic response in which titres persist despite cure.
questions.beyond_mandell: Gonorrhea and chlamydia regimens are from PHAC/CDC STI guidelines, not the Mandell syphilis chapter; note ceftriaxone for gonorrhea has been updated to 500 mg IM in recent PHAC/CDC guidance.

questions.model_answer: a) Three antibiotics: (1) Syphilis — benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose (documented seroconversion within 3 months = early syphilis). (2) Chlamydia — doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily for 7 days. (3) Gonorrhea — ceftriaxone 250 mg IM single dose. b) Two reasons for failure of a four-fold decline: (1) Reinfection. (2) Unrecognized neurosyphilis (or inadequate/failed treatment).
questions.beyond_mandell: Gonorrhea and chlamydia regimens are from PHAC/CDC STI guidelines, not the Mandell syphilis chapter; recent guidance raises the gonorrhea ceftriaxone dose to 500 mg IM.

cohort_answer.text:
Syphilis: Early (Primary, Secondary, early latent) - Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM x1. Late (Late latent, tertiary) - Benzathine Penicillin G 2.4 million units IM weekly x3. Neurosyphilis - Crystalline Pen G 4 million units q4h IV x14 days.
Chlamydia: Doxycycline 100mg PO BID x7 days.
Gonorrhea: Ceftriaxone 250mg IM x1.
If RPR not 4-fold decrease, 2 reasons: Recurrent infection; Neurosyphilis; Inadequate treatment.

questions.question: You are assessing a 1-day-old infant born to a mother with untreated Chlamydia trachomatis infection.
questions.question_raw: You are assessing a 1-day old infant born to a mother with untreated Chlamydia trachomatis infection.

parts.text: What prophylaxis or antiviral therapy, if any, does the infant require?
What are two classical clinical presentations of this infection that could present within a few weeks?
If the baby needs treatment, name the class of antimicrobial therapy you would use.

parts_raw.text: What prophylaxis or antiviral therapy, if any, does the infant require?
What are two classical clinical presentations of this infection that could present within a few weeks?
If the baby needs treatment, name the class of antimicrobial therapy you would use?

questions.model_answer:
a) No specific systemic prophylaxis is required or recommended; the routine topical erythromycin ointment given for gonococcal ophthalmia does NOT prevent perinatal C. trachomatis transmission. Monitor the infant clinically and treat if conjunctivitis or pneumonia develops.
b) (1) Neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis (ophthalmia neonatorum, watery-then-purulent discharge, onset ~5–12 days, up to 6 weeks). (2) Chlamydial infant pneumonia (afebrile, staccato cough, tachypnea, before 8 weeks of age).
c) Macrolide — oral erythromycin (50 mg/kg/day divided QID x 14 days).
questions.beyond_mandell: The "monitor rather than pre-emptively treat the asymptomatic exposed infant" approach reflects CDC/AAP guidance; the chapter states topical prophylaxis does not prevent transmission but does not detail management of the well exposed newborn.

questions.model_answer: Consider LGV (Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-L3). Investigations: NAAT for C. trachomatis with LGV-specific molecular testing on urine and rectal (+/- throat) specimens, and/or aspirate of a fluctuant lymph node; screen for concurrent HIV and other STIs. Treatment: doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x 21 days (alternative azithromycin) — aspirate fluctuant buboes rather than incise.

questions.question: State the preferred treatments for the following.
questions.question_raw: Preferred treatments: Chlamydia cervicitis in pregnancy; Group B strep ppx

parts.text: Chlamydia cervicitis in pregnancy
Group B streptococcus prophylaxis

parts_raw.text: Chlamydia cervicitis in pregnancy
Group B strep ppx

questions.model_answer:
a) Azithromycin 1 g PO single dose (CDC-recommended in pregnancy); alternatives are amoxicillin 500 mg PO tid x7 days or erythromycin, with a test of cure at 3-4 weeks. Doxycycline and fluoroquinolones are contraindicated.
b) Intrapartum penicillin G 5 million units IV then 2.5-3 million units q4h (or ampicillin 2 g IV then 1 g q4h) given at least 4 h before delivery; cefazolin 2 g IV then 1 g q8h for low-risk penicillin allergy. Screen at 35-37 weeks gestation.
questions.beyond_mandell: Group B streptococcus intrapartum prophylaxis is not covered in this Chlamydia chapter; part b rests on CDC/ACOG GBS prevention guidance.

cohort_answer.text: Chlamydia cervicitis in pregnancy: Azithromycin 1g PO x1 dose. Group B strep ppx: IV PenG 5mU or Ampicillin 2g IV or Cefazolin 2g IV at least 4h before birth. Risk factors for neonatal GBS sepsis: maternal colonization during current pregnancy, GBS bacteriuria, prior infant with invasive GBS disease, prolonged rupture of membranes, maternal fever. For colonization, risk of sepsis is 1-2%. Screen women at 35-37 weeks GA.
